title: Ranginui and Papatūānuku
source_ref: Māori tradition, in George Grey, Polynesian Mythology (1855), drawing on manuscripts by Wiremu Maihi Te Rangikāheke of Ngāti Rangiwewehi
paragraphs: In the Māori account, Ranginui the sky father and Papatūānuku the earth mother lay close together, and their many children lived in the darkness between them. There was no light, no room to stand, and no space for the world to grow. The children were gods: Tāne of the forest, Tangaroa of the sea, Tāwhirimātea of storms, and others.

The children argued about what to do. Some wanted to kill their parents, but Tāne proposed to separate them instead. He lay on his back between them and pushed upward with his legs. Slowly Ranginui rose above Papatūānuku, and light fell between them for the first time. Other tellings name different children and different methods.

Tāwhirimātea, god of storms, was furious. He had wanted his parents left as they were, and he refused to live in the new light. He went up to join his father in the sky and sent winds, clouds and rain against his brothers. He tore at Tāne's forests and lashed Tangaroa's sea, and the gods have been divided ever since.

Rongo and Haumia hid in the earth, where their plants still grow, and Tū stood his ground. Rangi and Papa grieve for each other; Rangi's tears fall as rain and dew, and Papa's sighs rise as mist. George Grey printed this account in 1855 from manuscripts by Te Rangikāheke, a Ngāti Rangiwewehi writer, and Māori iwi tell it with different names and emphases.
notes: Grey's 1855 text is the best-known English version, but it is a Victorian compilation from Māori manuscripts, especially Te Rangikāheke's. The number and names of the children, the method of separation, and the role of Whiro varies between iwi and between written collections; the grief of Rangi and Papa is elaborated differently in each.

title: Māui and the Sun
source_ref: Māori tradition, in Grey's Polynesian Mythology (1855); Hawaiian and other Polynesian versions differ in setting and detail
paragraphs: In the Māori story, the sun Tama-nui-te-rā crossed the sky too quickly. People had little time to fish, plant or cook before dusk, and Māui resolved to slow him down. He asked his brothers to help, and they gathered great lengths of flax rope, sometimes said to be woven from the hair of their sister Hina.

They travelled east to the pit where the sun sleeps at night. There they set nooses of rope around the opening and built a wall of clay to hide behind. When the sun rose, the ropes caught him. He struggled and the world shook, but the brothers held on, and Māui beat him with the jawbone of his grandmother Murirangawhenua.

At last the sun begged for mercy. Māui made him promise to move more slowly, so that days would be long enough for work and rest. The sun kept his word, and that is why the seasons turn at a gentler pace. Some versions add that the sun was wounded, and the taming is the usual ending.

Hawaiian tellings place the snaring on Haleakalā, where Māui uses a rope of coconut fibre and the sun agrees to slow down. Other Polynesian traditions give the trickster other names and make other bargains, and the details of the ropes change from island to island. The Māori version is the one George Grey printed in 1855, and it remains the best known.
notes: The Māori narrative is known from Grey and from later collections, and the ropes, the jawbone and the clay wall vary between tellings. Hawaiian versions are set at Haleakalā with different materials and bargains, and other island traditions credit the feat to other tricksters, so this retelling follows the Māori outline while noting the wider pattern.

title: Māui and the Fish
source_ref: Māori tradition, in Grey's Polynesian Mythology (1855); North Island place names and iwi variants
paragraphs: Māui's older brothers never let him join their fishing trips. One night he wove a strong flax line, recited a karakia over it, and hid in the hull of their canoe. When they were far out at sea, he climbed out. They refused him bait, so he struck his own nose and baited the hook with blood.

The hook was made from the jawbone of his grandmother Murirangawhenua. Māui lowered it into the deep and waited. Something enormous took it. He hauled and hauled, and the sea rose, and at last a great fish broke the surface. It was Hāhau-whenua, the fish that became Te Ika-a-Māui, the North Island.

Māui left his brothers to guard the fish while he went to find a tohunga to perform the proper ceremonies. They did not wait. They cut into the fish, and it writhed in pain, and its body broke into mountains, cliffs and valleys. That is why the North Island is rugged, and why people say it would have been flat.

The story is a map as well as a trickster tale. The North Island is Te Ika-a-Māui, the fish of Māui; the South Island is Te Waka-a-Māui, his canoe; and Rakiura is sometimes called the anchor stone. Southern iwi such as Kāi Tahu tell the land's origins differently, and their traditions deserve to be heard alongside this famous account.

title: Rata and the Forest
source_ref: Māori tradition (Grey 1855; the hākuturi) and Tahitian versions in Teuira Henry, Ancient Tahiti (1928)
paragraphs: Rata needed a canoe. His father had been killed, and he meant to travel and avenge him. He went into the forest, chose a tall tree, and cut it down without asking the forest god or performing the proper rites. He trimmed the trunk and left it lying, planning to return at dawn.

In the morning the tree stood upright again, whole and rooted, as if no axe had touched it. Rata cut it down a second time, and again it was restored. He hid and watched. At night a host of small forest creatures, the hākuturi, came and put every chip back in its place, singing as they worked.

Rata rushed out and caught them. They told him that he had insulted Tāne, god of the forest, by taking a tree without permission or ritual. Ashamed, Rata apologised. The hākuturi then shaped the trunk into a canoe for him, and it was a finer vessel than he could have made alone.

Tahitian versions tell the story differently. There the tree is guarded by forest spirits, and when Rata seizes them they build his canoe in a single night. In Māori accounts the creatures first restore the standing tree, then help. Both versions make the same point: the forest is not raw material, and a canoe begins with consent and ceremony.
notes: The Māori hākuturi are described variously as insects, birds or small spirits, and the canoe's name and Rata's parentage vary. Tahitian and Tuamotuan versions differ: the spirits build the canoe rather than restoring the tree, and Rata's motives and family change. This retelling follows the Māori outline and notes the Tahitian variant.

title: Pele and Kamapua'a
source_ref: Hawaiian tradition: Kepelino's Traditions of Hawaii (1860s-70s; edited by Martha Beckwith, 1932); G. W. Kahiolo, He Mo'olelo no Kamapua'a (1861); Martha Beckwith, Hawaiian Mythology (1940)
paragraphs: Kamapua'a was born on O'ahu to Hina and Kahikiula, a child who could take the shape of a pig or a man. He grew up bold, surfed, fought and travelled between islands. At last he came to Hawai'i Island and climbed to the rim of Kīlauea, where Pele, the volcano goddess, lay asleep in Halema'uma'u.

He stood on ground that was kapu, sacred to her, and chanted to wake her. Pele rose in anger. Fire leapt from the crater, and Kamapua'a answered with rain and flood. He tore at the land with his snout; she covered it with lava. Their quarrel shook the mountain and the sea around it.

Older tellings say the two became lovers before they fought, and that their contest was also a courtship. Neither could destroy the other. At last they made a truce and divided the island: Pele kept the dry leeward districts of Ka'ū and Kona, and Kamapua'a took the wet windward lands of Hilo, Hāmākua and Kohala.

For many Native Hawaiians, Pele is not a character in a tale but a living akua, honoured at Kīlauea, and her home is a sacred place. The story survives in Hawaiian-language newspapers and scholarly collections, and the versions differ: sometimes the pair marry, sometimes they part as enemies. This retelling keeps the contention and the divided island, and leaves the goddess her due.
notes: Kepelino, Kahiolo and Beckwith preserve different emphases: courtship, combat, and the division of the island. The boundary and the names of the districts vary, and Pele is a living deity for many Hawaiians, so the story is presented with care rather than as fiction.

title: Hina and the Eel
source_ref: Samoan (Sina and the Eel), Tahitian (Hina and Te Tuna) and Hawaiian (Hina and Kuna) traditions; Teuira Henry, Ancient Tahiti (1928); Beckwith, Hawaiian Mythology (1940)
paragraphs: Hina is identified with the moon in some Polynesian traditions and is a woman in others. In Tahiti she lived as the wife of Te Tuna, the eel god, beside the water. In time she tired of him and went inland to find another husband. Every man refused her, fearing the eel. At last she met Māui.

Te Tuna came after her, riding a great wave with four companions. Māui turned the wave back and drove them onto the reef. Then Te Tuna challenged Māui to a duel: each would shrink and enter the other's body to destroy him from within. Te Tuna tried first and failed.

Māui entered Te Tuna and tore him apart from inside. He cut off the eel's head and buried it, and a green shoot rose from the spot and grew into the first coconut tree. When people drink from a coconut, the three marks on its shell are called the eel's eyes and mouth.

The story changes shape across the Pacific. In Samoa the woman is Sina and the eel is Tui Fiti, the king of Fiji, who asks that his head be buried; the coconut grows from it. In Hawai'i, Hina is usually Māui's mother, and the watcher at the Wailuku River is a giant mo'o named Kuna, killed without any coconut. The Hina figures differ, and the coconut ending belongs to particular islands.
notes: Hina and Sina are related names attached to different figures: a moon deity, Māui's mother, and the wife of an eel god. The Tahitian and Samoan versions end with the first coconut, while the Hawaiian Hilo tradition has a mo'o named Kuna and no coconut origin. The narrative here follows the Tahitian sequence and marks the others in the final paragraph.
